nameStory: The red hake gets its name from its reddish-brown coloration that helps it blend in with the sandy and muddy ocean bottom. It's also called the 'squirrel hake' because of its reddish fur-like color and its habit of darting quickly into hiding spots when startled, much like a nervous squirrel scampering up a tree.
description: The red hake is a bottom-dwelling fish that lives in the deeper waters off New England's coast. It has an elongated, somewhat eel-like body that can grow up to 30 inches long and weigh around 7 pounds. Its most distinctive features are its reddish-brown color and the way its dorsal fin extends along most of its back. This is a popular fish among recreational anglers who enjoy the challenge of catching this tasty gamefish.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Reddish-brown to rusty coloration on the back and sides, fading to lighter tones on the belly - feels smooth and slightly slimy to the touch like most marine fish

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat compressed body that tapers toward the tail, giving it an almost eel-like appearance but much more robust

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal fin running along most of the back, with the second dorsal fin connecting almost to the tail fin, creating a continuous fin outline

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth (opens at the front tip of the head) with a slightly protruding lower jaw and small, sharp teeth that feel rough against your finger

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized fish typically 12-20 inches when caught, but can reach up to 30 inches and feel surprisingly heavy for their length

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper waters from 30 to 1,600 feet deep, often over sandy or muddy bottoms where they can burrow and hide

habitat: Red hake live in the deeper coastal waters of New England, typically found at depths between 30 and 1,600 feet over sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. They prefer the continental shelf waters from the Gulf of Maine down to southern New England. You won't find them in shallow tide pools or near shore - they're strictly a deep-water species that anglers target from boats in offshore waters.

seasonality.spring: Red hake begin moving into slightly shallower waters as temperatures warm, making them more accessible to deep-water anglers. This is when they start their spawning activities in deeper offshore areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for red hake, when they're feeding heavily in mid-depth waters. Prime fishing season for recreational anglers targeting them with bottom rigs in 100-300 foot depths.
seasonality.fall: Red hake continue feeding actively as they prepare for winter, often found in small schools over muddy bottoms. Water temperatures are still warm enough for good fishing success.
seasonality.winter: Red hake move to deeper waters and become less active in the coldest months. They're still present but harder to locate and less likely to bite, making winter the most challenging season for anglers.

funFact: Red hake are sometimes called 'living fishing lures' because they often swallow their prey so aggressively that smaller fish can sometimes be found still wriggling and alive inside a red hake's stomach when it's caught!
confusionNotes: Red hake are most commonly confused with white hake, but red hake have that distinctive reddish-brown color while white hake are grayish. Memory trick: 'Red hake = reddish color, white hake = whitish-gray color' - the names actually match the colors!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hake,' red hake are actually in the Phycidae family, not the true hake family (Merlucciidae). This naming confusion comes from their similar bottom-dwelling lifestyle and elongated body shape, but they're more closely related to cods than to true hakes.
compareHints: Red hake can be distinguished from their close relatives by color - they're much more reddish than the grayish white hake or the spotted pattern of spotted hake. Red hake also tend to be found in slightly deeper waters than spotted hake, and they lack the distinctive spots that give spotted hake their name. All three species share the elongated body and continuous dorsal fin, but the red hake's rusty coloration is usually unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike red hake which has a reddish tint and white hake which is more uniformly colored, spotted hake is the only one in the genus with distinct dark spots.
White Hake is the palest of the three Urophycis species in New England waters - much lighter than the reddish-brown Red Hake and lacking the distinctive spots of the Spotted Hake.
